newsitem.title: INDIA: Quake strikes heart of India, killing dozens.
newsitem.headline: Quake strikes heart of India, killing dozens.

text.p: At least 38 people were killed and more than 1,000 injured when an earthquake struck central India early on Thursday, flattening houses and burying many victims as they slept, officials said.

The earthquake, which measured 6.0 on the Richter scale and lasted about 50 seconds, rocked Madhya Pradesh state in the heart of the subcontinent at 4.22 a.m. (2252 GMT Wednesday), authorities in Jabalpur city said.
Hospital officials in Jabalpur, 260 km (160 miles) southeast of the state capital Bhopal, said 38 people were killed and at least 1,000 injured. Many victims died when their houses collapsed on them.
Authorities said 188 people were in serious condition in hospital. Most sustained head and spinal injuries or broken bones.
Officials said they did not expect the death toll to rise significantly but they noted that rescuers had yet to reach many remote villages more than 12 hours after the quake.

United News of India said the district administration had asked the army to help with rescue and relief work. It said the quake toppled telephone and power lines in some areas, disrupting electricity supplies and cutting off some towns.

The earthquake was centred on the village of Kosamghat, 23 km (14 miles) south of Jabalpur. All the village's 160 houses, mostly mud huts, were flattened, leaving more than 1,000 residents homeless, elder Mohan Lal Yadav said.

Forty villagers were injured but no one was killed because people were sleeping outside in the early summer heat. "Had this been a winter night, not a single person would have survived," said 65-year-old Shanti Bal.
In nearby Donda Mehgaon village, four people were killed and numerous water buffaloes, used to produce milk or work in the wheat fields, were crushed in their sheds, residents said.

Villagers, some of them crying, sheltered from the hot sun under trees and were brought food and water from other villages. The quake had muddied waters drawn from wells at Donda Mehgaon and Kosamghat.
In September 1993, about 10,000 people were killed in neighbouring Maharashtra state when an earthquake measuring 6.3 on the Richter scale struck the Latur-Osmanabad region.

A seismology department official in New Delhi said the quake in Latur was much closer to the surface than the one in Madhya Pradesh, making it more deadly. In addition, the soil in central India was more solid.
The quake was felt across a wide swathe of northern, central and eastern India and woke up people in the capital New Delhi, 720 km (450 miles) to the northwest.
"When the earthquake struck, it was like the sound of machines in factories," said Rajendra Bhatia, marketing manager for a pharmaceuticals firm in Jabalpur.
"The first noise of the earthquake was like a jet sweeping over us," oil trader Sandeep Kumar Sahu said.

The quake was centred at latitude 23.1 degrees north and longitude 80.1 degrees east, putting it in the Narmada River basin where five earthquakes of at least 6.0 on the Richter scale have occurred since 1927, the Press Trust of India said.

An official statement said Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral expressed anguish and grief over the devastation and told a top official to coordinate relief and rescue measures with the state government.

The federal government released 101 million rupees ($2.8 million) in calamity relief, while the Madhya Pradesh government said it would pay 100,000 rupees to the families of the deceased and between 2,000 and 10,000 rupees to the injured.
